explanations.text:
import the code reader of python, the line matcher, json, the shell, and
[the map run](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py) — the neighbour that saves one entry

ANCHOR_RE      = the look of a pin: the words in square brackets, the target in parentheses
SYNC_PROMPT    = the letter to claude when the code changed: read the whole file, mend the words the change made wrong, and add a sentence for each behaviour the change added
STALE_PROMPT   = the letter to claude when a parent abstraction changed: mend the child's wrong words and carry the new facts down
PAGE_IMPORT_RE = the look of an import in a web page: a from with a path, or a script with a src


finding the pieces of a file

[block_spans](block_spans)(path, lines)
    path is the file on disk; lines is its text, one line each.
    The tool finds every named piece of the file and the lines it covers, so a
    pin can only point at a real piece. A markdown file gives its headings, a web
    page its once-only tags and its functions, a python file its functions and
    classes — read by python's own reader of code. Any other file has no pieces.

[md_spans](md_spans)(path, lines)
    Every heading is a piece that runs to the next heading of the same or a
    higher level. Headings inside a code fence do not count. Two headings with
    the same words stop the run, because a name must point at one place.

[html_spans](html_spans)(path, lines)
    The pieces of a web page, from two hands: [the once-only tags](tag_spans) — a
    tag that opens once, from its opening line to its closing line — and the named
    functions inside every script ([the script regions](script_regions) says where
    the scripts are). A function with the name of a tag stops the run.

[js_spans](js_spans)(path, lines, regions)
    regions are the line ranges of the scripts.
    The tool walks each script, notes where a function starts, and counts the
    braces line by line ([the brace count](brace_delta), which skips braces inside
    quotes and after //) to know where it ends. A function named twice stops the run.


checking the pins of a text

[build_anchors](build_anchors)(text, data, spans, self_id, folder)
    text is one abstraction; data is the map of the file; spans are its pieces;
    self_id is the entry the text belongs to; folder is the project root.
    The tool takes the pins one by one. The words must be there and appear once
    in the text. A pin into the code goes to [the resolving](resolve_code_target);
    a pin into an earlier abstraction must name an entry that exists, an anchor it
    holds, and never its own entry. It gives back the list of checked pins, each
    with its lines. One bad pin stops with the reason.

[parse_target](parse_target)(raw)
    raw is what stands in the parentheses of a pin.
    `e3:the start` is a pin into entry 3's anchor; anything else names a piece
    or a file.

[resolve_code_target](resolve_code_target)(words, raw, spans, folder)
    A piece of this file wins first. Then `file:piece` — a piece of another file
    of the project. Then a file of the project on its own. Anything else stops.

[check_cycle](check_cycle)(data, self_id, anchors)
    The tool follows the pins into earlier abstractions, and theirs, and stops
    when the chain comes back to the entry itself. A telling may not stand on
    itself.

[project_pins](project_pins)(anchors)
    The pins of the project's own map must all name a file or a piece of a file.


the commands

[cmd_retext](cmd_retext)(a)
    a is what you typed: the file, the entry id, and the text or --text.
    You type `human retext file 2 --text words.txt`.
    The tool checks the new text like a new entry, and one thing more: every
    anchor another entry points at must still be there. Then it puts the text in
    place and marks each entry that points into it stale, so they can be mended
    on your word.

[cmd_undo](cmd_undo)(a)
    The tool removes the last entry of the map. An entry that others point
    into stays until they go first.

[cmd_show](cmd_show)(a)
    You type `human show file`, or `human show .` for the whole project.
    The tool lists every entry — id, piece, lines, pins, stale or not — and
    warns for every pin that no longer fits its lines, names a piece or a file
    that is gone, or points at an anchor that is gone. For a python file it
    reads [the imported names](import_names) — plain imports and the `from .`
    ones of the same folder — and warns when a mapped neighbour has no pin in the
    whole-file entry. For the project it adds [the doubled lines](dup_warnings):
    a line of thirty letters or more that stands in the maps of two files, compared
    with pins and punctuation stripped ([the bare line](norm_dup)). Then it says how
    much of the file is covered.

[cmd_lines](cmd_lines)(a)
    The file with a number in front of every line.

[cmd_sync](cmd_sync)(a)
    You type `human sync file`, or `--old copy.py` when the last version does
    not live in git, or `--stale 3` to mend one dependent entry.
    For the project map the tool only re-resolves the file pins and reports the
    gone ones. For a file that did not change it re-resolves the cross-file pins
    and stops. Otherwise it holds [the old lines](old_lines_of) next to the new
    ones, sees where each line went ([the line map](line_map)), and finds the
    candidates: every entry whose lines ([the lines of an entry](entry_lines_set))
    the change touched, plus every entry whose piece is gone. It carries every
    entry and pin to its new lines ([the re-resolving](re_resolve), with
    [the refresh of a file pin](refresh_file_anchor) for pins into other files).
    With no candidate it saves and stops — no claude call. With candidates it
    writes the letter — the diff, the path of the file to read whole,
    [the line about the neighbours](touched_note) the file imports, the pieces,
    the candidate texts, the anchors they must keep — and asks claude, up to
    --tries times. Each answer is tried on a copy of the map
    ([the rebuild](rebuild_all)): renamed pieces, new texts, every pin checked,
    every needed anchor kept. One broken rule goes back to claude with its name.
    The first good answer is saved, and the entries that point into a changed one
    are marked stale. A candidate that got new lines but kept all its words gets
    a warning that names [the pieces the new lines fall in](blocks_of).

[repair_stale](repair_stale)(a, code_path, root, map_path, data, lines, spans)
    The tool takes one stale entry, the old and new text of the parent it
    stands on, the diff between the two, and the anchors it must keep, and asks
    claude for the mended child text, up to --tries times. Each answer passes
    the pin checks. The first good one is saved and its own dependents are
    marked stale.

[ask_claude](ask_claude)(prompt, root)
    One call to claude with the letter; the answer is read as one JSON object.
    The call runs in the project root, so claude can open the files the letter
    names. A failed call stops the run.


──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
the small hands

[numbered](numbered)(lines)                   the lines with a number in front
[import_names](import_names)(lines)           the names a python file imports
[sibling_imports](sibling_imports)(code_path, lines, root)
                                              the files of the project this file imports, from a python
                                              file or from a web page
[blocks_of](blocks_of)(lines, spans, code_name)
                                              the pieces a set of lines falls in
[touched_note](touched_note)(code_path, old, new, root)
                                              the letter's line about the neighbours, with the ones the
                                              change added and removed
[norm_dup](norm_dup)(line)                    a line with pins and punctuation stripped, lowercase
[expand](expand)(span_list)                   every line number inside a list of ranges
[fmt](fmt)(nums)                              line numbers as "3-5, 9"
[children_of](children_of)(data, eid)         the entries that point into entry eid
[needed_words](needed_words)(data, eid)       the anchors of entry eid that other entries point at
[mark_children](mark_children)(data, eid, old_text)
                                              marks the dependents stale, with the old parent text
[recompute](recompute)(data, lines)           which lines the map covers and which it does not
[guard_structure](guard_structure)(data, map_path)
                                              stops on a map of the old kind
[find_root](find_root)(path)                  the folder at or above path that holds human/human.json
[rel_name](rel_name)(code_path, root)         the path of a file from the root, like src/app.py
[map_path_of](map_path_of)(code_path, root)   the map file of a code file: human/explanation_<path>.json,
                                              the slashes written as __
[register_file](register_file)(root, rel)     adds a file to the list in human/human.json
[load_existing](load_existing)(code_path)     the map of a file, or a stop when there is none
[read_text_arg](read_text_arg)(a)             the text from --text or from the pipe; a stop when empty
[anchor_counts](anchor_counts)(anchors)       "7 anchors (5 into the code, 2 into earlier explanations)"
[print_coverage](print_coverage)(missing, blank, lines)
                                              "covered: 61 of 63 code lines" and the lines left
[report_text_diff](report_text_diff)(eid, old, new)
                                              the changed lines of an entry, - old and + new

explanations.text:
The tool first looks at the end of the file's name,
  because each kind of file names its pieces its own way.

  A code file, ending in .py:
      a piece is a part of the code with a name of its own —
      a function definition, or a class.
      The tool does not read the code by itself. It hands the
      file to a library: a ready-made helper that ships with
      the language. The library looks at the code without
      running it, and it knows the grammar of the language,
      so it finds every function and every class, where each
      one starts, where it ends, and what sits inside what.
      That is why the pieces are exact, never guessed.
      A file the library cannot read gives no pieces.

  A document, ending in .md:
      a piece is a section under a heading.
      It runs until the next heading of its rank or higher.
      A heading inside a [fenced example](md_spans) does not count.
      Two headings with the same words are refused,
      because a name must hold one thing only.

  A web page, ending in .html:
      the pieces come from two places.
      A tag that appears one time only — head, style, body —
      is a piece, from where it opens to where it closes.
      And every named function inside a script is a piece,
      the nested ones too, found by counting the braces
      that open and close around them.
      A function that carries the name of a tag is refused.

  Any other kind of file gives no pieces at all.

A document can hold an example: a stretch of text shown
  exactly as it is, the way a book quotes a letter.
  A fence marks it: a line of three marks — ``` or ~~~ —
  opens the example, and the same line of marks closes it.

  Inside the fences, nothing is really said — it is only
  shown. A line in there that looks like a heading is just
  a picture of a heading. So the tool passes over it: it
  does not become a piece, and it does not end the section
  it sits in.

  The tool reads the document line by line. At an opening
  fence it stops taking headings, and at the closing fence
  it takes them again.
